asDecan.p: Every sign is split into three ten-degree slices, called decans, and each slice has a ruling planet and a small card of its own. Your Sun falls somewhere between ten and nineteen degrees of Cancer, the middle slice, and the Golden Dawn gives that stretch to Mercury. The middle of a sign is where it has settled in and is at full strength, so the feeling in you is deep and it's been there a long while. Mercury gets no special standing in Cancer. It's a visitor, neither helped nor held back, and it takes on the colour of the Moon, which rules the sign. So your thinking and your talking run on feeling and on memory. The Two of Cups before you belongs to Venus and is all about one other person. The Four after you belongs to the Moon and goes quiet. Yours is the chatty one in between. The Chariot is still your Sun card, and this is the finer grain of it. Have a look at the three women in the picture, cups up, clearly halfway through a story.

You're the one who knows everybody's news. Your cousin's IVF, the neighbour's new job, which of your school friends isn't speaking to which, and you didn't go looking for any of it, people just tell you. The family group chat would go dead within a week if you left it. At a birthday lunch you'll be halfway through a story about something that happened in 1998, with names and who wore what, and someone will ask how on earth you remember that. You remember because it mattered to you at the time. Late at night you replay conversations, sometimes whole ones, trying to work out what she meant when she said 'fine'. And on a Sunday with nothing planned you end up on the phone for two hours without quite meaning to.

The gift that doesn't get talked about is that you can put feeling into words for other people. Mercury in this sign works as a translator. When a friend has to write the hard email to their father, they send you the draft first, and you're the one who finds the sentence that says what they meant without starting a war. You get asked to give the speech at the fortieth, or the eulogy, and you're good at it because you've quietly kept the stories for years. I see this a lot in the middle of Cancer. There's a knack for saying the soft thing so nobody's embarrassed, and for knowing the point in a conversation when someone is finally ready to hear it. Families lean on that more than they know.

News is how you bond, and that's where it can slip. Someone tells you something in confidence, and a few days later you've told someone else. There was no malice in it. Passing things along is how you feel close to people, and in the moment it felt like care. The other side of this is that you can talk about a feeling for so long that you never quite have it. You'll describe the breakup to six friends, a bit funnier each time, and the story gets polished while the hurt sits underneath untouched. Family history gets the same treatment. You've told the version where your dad was difficult so many times that it's hard to see him any other way, and your sister, who remembers it differently, stopped arguing years ago.

Stress sends you to the phone. The first thing you do after bad news is ring someone, then someone else, and by the end of the evening four people know and you've said it so often it has started to feel manageable. That part works. A week later the talking has usually turned into circling. You're awake at two going over the same conversation, drafting replies you'll never send, asking everyone the same question in slightly different words. Friends start to feel they're giving advice into a hole, and your partner hears the story for the ninth time and goes a bit glassy. What helps is less talk and more body. Cook something that takes an hour. Swim, or walk until you're tired. Then tell one person, once, what you actually feel, and let them sit with you without fixing it.

You fall for people through talking. The first date that goes on until the staff start stacking chairs is usually the one. What's less obvious is how much it matters to you that a partner fits in with your people. This is a card with three people in it, and your love life tends to happen inside a circle, so if your best friend doesn't warm to someone, or your mum goes a bit quiet about them, it gets under your skin more than you'd like. The harder habit is your memory. In an argument you can quote back exactly what they said last March, and you're usually right, which doesn't help at all. Cancer's opposite is Capricorn, and a steadier partner who says less can feel like a wall at first. Give them time. Some people show it in what they do.

You're wasted in a job where nobody talks to you. Mercury wants words and Cancer wants people it cares about, so the good fits tend to be where those two overlap. Teaching, counselling, community radio, writing about food or family or a particular town, running the local newsletter, being the office manager everyone brings their problems to. A lot of people with the Sun here end up holding the institutional memory, the one who knows why the policy exists and who fell out with whom in 2014. That's valuable, and it's worth getting it written into your role and your pay. The trap is the long chat by the kettle that eats your afternoon, followed by staying late to catch up. Guard a couple of hours a day with the door shut.

At twenty this slice tends to be all talk and a lot of heart. Big friend groups, long phone calls, a habit of taking on everyone's drama as if it were your own, and a friendship or two lost to something said in the wrong room. By the mid-thirties most people with the Sun here have got choosier about who they tell what, and the circle turns into the kind of friends you'd trust with a key to the house. The storytelling gets better too, because there's more to tell and you've learned to leave out the bits that aren't yours. The fifties often hand you the job of family historian. You're the one with the photos, the recipes and the names pencilled on the back of the prints, and younger relatives start ringing to ask what their grandmother was like.

Pick one conversation a week where you only ask and listen. Coffee with a friend, a phone call with a parent. Don't pass on any news of your own or anyone else's, and don't tell a story unless they ask for one. Notice how often you want to jump in with 'that reminds me'. Afterwards, write down one thing you learned about them that you didn't know before, on paper, and keep the list somewhere you'll see it.
